These are **optional, selected worked examples**, not an answer to every question or an assessment rubric. Each panel corresponds to a named section of the learning materials. Try the question independently before opening the panel.

Most examples use the `refugees` package, whose contents may change between releases. **Run the code on your installed data rather than treating any numerical result in an older version as permanent.** In particular, check reporting categories and missing values before interpreting a country total.

The examples below presume that the packages required for the relevant exercises have been installed. To run several examples together in a fresh R session, first load:

```{r}
library(refugees)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Getting started · Installing versus loading, scripts, and projects"}

- `install.packages("dplyr")` downloads and installs a package in your R library; you generally do this only when setting up or updating the package.
- `library(dplyr)` makes an installed package's functions directly available **in the current R session**.
- The **Console** executes instructions immediately; a saved **script** records the steps you want to rerun.
- An **RStudio project** keeps scripts and data together so you can use relative paths, such as `data/file.csv`.

After restarting R, a reproducible script should load its packages and create its objects anew. A variable that existed only in the previous session's Environment cannot be assumed to exist again.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Run this in the Console when you need to inspect the setup
sessionInfo()
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="First steps in R · Objects, vectors, functions, and missing values"}

```{r}
recognitions <- c(8, 11, 3, 15, 9)

c(total = sum(recognitions),
  minimum = min(recognitions),
  maximum = max(recognitions),
  median = median(recognitions))

recognitions[3] <- NA
mean(recognitions)                # NA: an input is missing
mean(recognitions, na.rm = TRUE) # Mean of the four observed values
sum(is.na(recognitions))         # Number of missing entries
```

An **object** has a name, such as `recognitions`; the **vector** is the sequence of values stored in that object. A function such as `mean()` receives an **argument**. `na.rm = TRUE` changes how missing values are handled, not the original data. If the missing observations are systematically different, the calculated mean may be misleading.

`applications[1]` selects by **position**, while `applications[applications > 15]` selects by a **condition**. `=` inside a function call names an argument; `<-` assigns an object; `==` tests equality.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Meet the UNHCR data · Origin, destination, and unit of observation"}

- `coo_name` and `coo_iso` identify **origin**; `coa_name` and `coa_iso` identify **country of asylum/destination**.
- The `refugees` variable in `population` is an **end-of-year stock** in that category. `asylum_seekers` is another stock, **not** the number of applications filed during that year.
- The population table commonly contains several **origin–destination–year** records for the same destination. A destination total must be carefully aggregated over included origins.
- In `asylum_decisions`, `dec_rejected` counts recorded rejections and `dec_other` refers to other protection outcomes. Their interpretation still depends on procedure, stage, and cases-versus-persons coding.

```{r}
refugees::population |>
  filter(year == 2022, coa_iso == "ESP") |>
  select(year, coo_name, coa_name, refugees, asylum_seekers) |>
  head(5)
```

This shows **five records**, not five people, and not necessarily the five most important origins.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Data transformation · Aggregating origins rather than destinations"}

To answer *How many refugees from each origin were reported across included destinations in 2022?*, group by **origin**, not by destination:

```{r}
origins_2022 <- refugees::population |>
  filter(year == 2022, !is.na(coo_iso)) |>
  group_by(coo_iso, coo_name) |>
  summarise(
    n_missing = sum(is.na(refugees)),
    refugee_stock = if (all(is.na(refugees))) NA_real_ else
      sum(refugees, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(refugee_stock))

head(origins_2022)
```

This sums **reported external stocks** for an origin across included destinations. It is **not** a measure of the internally displaced population in that origin country. An all-missing group stays missing rather than being silently converted to zero; partially missing groups still require caution.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Data transformation · Wide and long formats"}

A **wide** table might have `destination`, `2020`, `2021`, `2022` as columns. After `pivot_longer()`, one row represents a **destination–year**, with the year stored in a variable.

```{r}
example_wide <- tibble(
  destination = c("Germany", "Spain"),
  `2020` = c(100, 50),
  `2021` = c(120, 75)
)

example_long <- example_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`2020`, `2021`),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "applications",
    names_transform = list(year = as.integer)
  )

example_wide_again <- example_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = applications)

example_long
example_wide_again
```

Reshaping **rearranges** values; it does not add application records. With a real UNHCR population table, aggregate origin-specific rows to a unique destination–year **before** pivoting to one year per column. Adding annual stock columns would incorrectly sum stocks measured at different dates.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Descriptive statistics · Means, medians, skewness, and shares"}

```{r}
origins <- read_csv("data/unhcr_origin_top10_2022.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
x <- origins$refugees_plus_oip / 1e6

c(mean = mean(x), median = median(x), sd = sd(x),
  minimum = min(x), maximum = max(x), IQR = IQR(x))

origins |>
  filter(refugees_plus_oip > mean(refugees_plus_oip)) |>
  select(origin, refugees_plus_oip)
```

These summaries describe only the **selected ten origins**, not the typical origin worldwide. A long right tail tends to pull the mean upward relative to the median, but the shape is best checked using a distribution plot.

For the destination top-five share, the denominator is the sum of **all included destination totals in the derived table**, not the world's annual asylum applications. If all contributing origin counts are missing for a destination, do not recode that destination to zero without explanation.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Visualization · Bar charts, distributions, and skewness"}

```{r}
hosts_2022 <- refugees::population |>
  filter(year == 2022, !is.na(coa_iso)) |>
  group_by(coa_iso, coa_name) |>
  summarise(
    missing_origins = sum(is.na(refugees)),
    refugee_stock = if (all(is.na(refugees))) NA_real_ else
      sum(refugees, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

top10 <- hosts_2022 |>
  filter(!is.na(refugee_stock)) |>
  slice_max(order_by = refugee_stock, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot(top10,
       aes(x = refugee_stock / 1e6,
           y = reorder(coa_name, refugee_stock))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2475a6") +
  labs(x = "Reported refugee stock (millions)", y = NULL,
       title = "Largest recorded destination totals in 2022",
       caption = "Source: refugees::population; special reporting categories and missingness require review") +
  theme_minimal()
```

`geom_col()` displays **already calculated numerical totals**. `geom_bar()` instead counts the **number of rows** by default. A histogram of `hosts_2022$refugee_stock` counts **destinations per bin**, not refugees per bin. The boxplot's distant observations are not automatically errors.

A right-skewed distribution has a longer **right-hand tail**. A log scale can make strongly unequal positive values easier to compare, but requires stating which zeros/missing values were excluded.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Time trends · Absolute change, percentage change, and indices"}

Take a fictional end-of-year stock of 100,000 in 2015, 120,000 in 2016 and 90,000 in 2017:

| Year | Stock | Change from previous year | Percentage change from previous year | Index (2015 = 100) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2015 | 100,000 | — | — | 100 |
| 2016 | 120,000 | +20,000 | +20% | 120 |
| 2017 | 90,000 | −30,000 | −25% | 90 |

The index of **90** in 2017 means the stock is **10% below 2015**, not that it fell by 10% from 2016.

```{r}
stock_example <- tibble(year = 2015:2017, stock = c(100000, 120000, 90000)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(
    previous_year = lag(year),
    previous_stock = lag(stock),
    absolute_change = if_else(year - previous_year == 1,
                              stock - previous_stock, NA_real_),
    pct_change = if_else(year - previous_year == 1 & previous_stock > 0,
                         100 * (stock / previous_stock - 1), NA_real_),
    index_2015 = 100 * stock / first(stock)
  )

stock_example
```

For real country data, sort and calculate `lag()` **within each country**, and check that consecutive rows are consecutive years. Differences in recorded stocks are **not counts of new arrivals**.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Applications and decisions · Choosing the substantive denominator"}

```{r}
toy <- read_csv("data/toy_asylum_decisions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

toy_rates <- toy |>
  mutate(
    substantive = recognized + other_protection + rejected,
    recognition_pct = if_else(substantive > 0,
      100 * recognized / substantive, NA_real_),
    protection_pct = if_else(substantive > 0,
      100 * (recognized + other_protection) / substantive, NA_real_),
    closed_in_denominator = if_else(substantive + closed > 0,
      100 * (recognized + other_protection) / (substantive + closed), NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(country, substantive, recognition_pct,
         protection_pct, closed_in_denominator)

toy_rates
```

For the **fictional Albia** values specified in the exercise (45 recognized, 15 other protection, 40 rejected), the recognition rate is **45%** and total protection rate is **60%**. Including `closed` changes the quantity being measured. Do not compare those toy rates with real country performance.

A share among this year's substantive decisions is **not** an applicant's lifetime probability of recognition: decisions made this year need not concern applications made this year.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Joins · Matches, duplicate keys, and reporting coverage"}

**Do not** sum all applications across procedural types and reporting units and present the result as a country-level asylum indicator. The join exercise instead asks where **records are available**.

```{r}
# Recreate the destination table here so this example can run independently.
hosts_2022 <- refugees::population |>
  filter(year == 2022, !is.na(coa_iso)) |>
  group_by(coa_iso, coa_name) |>
  summarise(refugee_stock = if (all(is.na(refugees))) NA_real_ else
              sum(refugees, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

app_coverage <- refugees::asylum_applications |>
  filter(year == 2022, !is.na(coa_iso), !is.na(applied)) |>
  group_by(coa_iso) |>
  summarise(n_application_rows = n(), .groups = "drop")

# A destination code must be unique in both tables for a one-to-one join.
hosts_2022 |>
  count(coa_iso) |>
  filter(n > 1)

app_coverage |>
  count(coa_iso) |>
  filter(n > 1)

matched <- hosts_2022 |>
  left_join(app_coverage, by = "coa_iso")

sum(is.na(matched$n_application_rows))

hosts_2022 |>
  anti_join(app_coverage, by = "coa_iso") |>
  select(coa_iso, coa_name)
```

If the first uniqueness check finds repeated destination codes, inspect the code/name definitions and fix the destination key **before** interpreting the joined result. A missing match means no matching reporting row under these filters, **not** necessarily zero applications. For a multi-year join, use both `coa_iso` **and** `year`.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Regression · Reading and checking an OLS result"}

The inference exercises use **160 invented jurisdictions** with `staff_per_100`, `complexity`, `resources`, and `processing_months` (as defined in [Inference](09-inference.qmd)). Run the data-generation block there first. Then:

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_simple <- lm(processing_months ~ staff_per_100, data = jurisdictions)
m_adjusted <- lm(processing_months ~ staff_per_100 + complexity + resources,
                 data = jurisdictions)

summary(m_simple)
coef(m_simple)
confint(m_simple)

# Reproduce the simple-model slope from covariance / variance
cov(jurisdictions$staff_per_100,
    jurisdictions$processing_months) / var(jurisdictions$staff_per_100)

# Extract the estimate, standard error, p-value and 95% interval
broom::tidy(m_adjusted, conf.int = TRUE)
```

**The coefficient's units are months per one additional staff member per 100 pending cases.** `summary()` also displays standard errors, test statistics, p-values, and $R^2$. A 95% confidence interval expresses uncertainty **under assumptions of the statistical procedure**; it is not a 95% probability that a fixed true coefficient lies in this particular interval. Changes between model specifications do not automatically identify a causal effect.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Logistic regression · Log-odds, odds ratios, and predicted probabilities"}

Use the **fictional claims dataset** generated in [Inference](09-inference.qmd), or the optional lab. Run its generation block before using the following code:

```{r}
#| eval: false
logit_model <- glm(
  recognized ~ represented + evidence_index + origin_group,
  data = claims,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

# Log-odds coefficients
coef(logit_model)

# Exponentiate to obtain odds ratios
exp(coef(logit_model))

# Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals
broom::tidy(logit_model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)

# Two otherwise identical profiles, differing in representation
profiles <- data.frame(
  represented = c(0, 1),
  evidence_index = c(0, 0),
  origin_group = factor(c("A", "A"), levels = levels(claims$origin_group))
)
profiles$probability <- predict(logit_model,
                                newdata = profiles, type = "response")
100 * diff(profiles$probability)  # Difference in percentage points
```

A logistic coefficient is a difference in **log-odds**, and `exp(coefficient)` is an **odds ratio**. An odds ratio of 2 does **not** imply twice the probability or a 100-percentage-point difference. Predicted probabilities depend on the covariate profile.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Regression tables · Exporting and labeling model output"}

Once `m_simple` and `m_adjusted` exist, you can compare them in a publication-style table. The example below is **optional**, since it requires `stargazer` to be installed.

```{r}
#| eval: false
stargazer::stargazer(
  m_simple, m_adjusted,
  type = "text", digits = 3,
  column.labels = c("Simple", "Adjusted")
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Simple" = m_simple, "Adjusted" = m_adjusted),
  output = "outputs/ols-models.html"
)
```

A responsible table identifies the outcome, coefficient units, observations, controls, uncertainty measure (for example **standard errors in parentheses**), and whether estimates are descriptive. For logistic models, explicitly say whether entries show **log-odds coefficients** or **odds ratios**.

:::

## Before using an answer in your own analysis

A correct command and a plausible number do not by themselves produce a valid research claim. State the **data source, unit of observation, year, population category, procedural coverage, missing-data treatment, numerator and denominator (if applicable)**. For regression, also identify the model specification and uncertainty assumptions. These worked examples are intended for practice and do not constitute UNHCR or RefLex research findings.
